task_4.title: Enable async class-based view handlers
task_4.description: Flask 2.0.2 fixes class-based routing so `View` and `MethodView` instances can use async handler methods the same way function-based views already can. Requests to routes registered from these classes should execute async handlers through Flask's sync bridge instead of surfacing coroutine return errors.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that routes created from class-based views support async handlers so applications can use async `View` and `MethodView` methods without failing at request time.

expectation.grounded: When a route is registered from `View.as_view(...)`, an async `dispatch_request` must be executed through `current_app.ensure_sync(...)` before its result is processed as the response. When a route is registered from `MethodView.as_view(...)`, the selected method handler such as `get` or `post` must likewise be executed through Flask's sync bridge so async methods behave like async function-based views instead of returning an unawaited coroutine.
expectation.conceptual: Class-based views should support async request handlers just like regular Flask view functions. If a `View` or `MethodView` handler is declared with `async def`, requests should complete normally and produce the handler's response rather than failing because a coroutine object was returned.

constraints.grounded: The change must preserve existing `View` and `MethodView` dispatch semantics, including normal method selection for `MethodView` and the existing assertion when no handler exists for the request method. Synchronous handlers must continue to work without behavior changes, and the request should still yield a normal Flask response value after sync-wrapping.
constraints.conceptual: Async support for class-based views must be additive and must not regress existing synchronous class-based views or normal HTTP method dispatch behavior.

behavior: A `View` subclass may implement `dispatch_request` as an async handler and still be used with `as_view(...)` in `add_url_rule(...)`.
A `MethodView` subclass may implement verb-specific handlers such as `get` or `post` as async handlers and have them invoked correctly for incoming requests.
Requests to routes backed by async class-based handlers should resolve to the handler's returned response value instead of exposing a coroutine object to Flask's response validation.
The async support path for class-based handlers should match the application-level sync bridging already used for async function-based views.
acceptance_criteria: When a route is registered from a `View` subclass whose `dispatch_request` is `async def`, sending a request to that route should return the handler's response successfully.
When a route is registered from a `MethodView` subclass with async HTTP verb handlers, sending requests for supported methods should return each handler's response successfully.
When an async class-based handler returns a valid Flask response value, the request should not fail due to Flask treating the result as a coroutine.
When a synchronous `View` or `MethodView` handler is used, it should continue to behave as before.

task_2.title: Correct callback type annotations for request hooks and related APIs
task_2.description: Flask 2.0.2 aligns its public type annotations with documented callback behavior. Request hook decorators that may short-circuit request handling are now typed to allow response return values, first-request hooks remain typed as return-ignored callbacks, and several related callback aliases are broadened or corrected for static type checking.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Flask's public typing for request lifecycle decorators and related callback APIs matches their documented behavior, especially so that `before_request` and `before_app_request` handlers may legally return a response-like value to stop further request handling while first-request hooks remain return-ignored.

expectation.grounded: The public callable types used by `before_request` and `before_app_request` must accept zero-argument handlers whose return type is either `None` or any valid `ResponseReturnValue`. The callable types used by `before_first_request` and `before_app_first_request` must remain zero-argument handlers returning `None`. Related public typing must also reflect that teardown callbacks return `None`, template filters and globals may accept arbitrary arguments, template tests may accept arbitrary arguments and return `bool`, and error-handler typing should preserve the handled exception type while still returning a valid `ResponseReturnValue`.
expectation.conceptual: Applications using Flask 2.0.2 should see static type hints that match actual framework contracts for hooks and callback registration. Request-preprocessing hooks can either continue normally or return a response to end processing, while callbacks whose return values are ignored should be typed that way instead of implying unsupported behavior.

constraints.grounded: This update must not change the documented runtime semantics of the decorators or callback registration APIs. `before_first_request` and `before_app_first_request` must not be treated as response-producing hooks, and request hook decorators must continue accepting handlers with no parameters. Any allowed return values for `before_request` and `before_app_request` are limited to existing `ResponseReturnValue` forms or `None`.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade is a typing-contract correction, not a behavioral redesign. Existing hook execution rules should stay the same, and only the public developer-facing type expectations should be brought into line with what the framework already documents and supports.

behavior: `before_request`-registered handlers are typed as zero-argument callables that may return `None` or a valid response value that short-circuits request handling.
`before_app_request` uses the same response-capable hook typing as `before_request`.
`before_first_request` and `before_app_first_request` are typed separately from request hooks and continue to represent zero-argument callbacks whose return values are ignored.
Teardown callbacks are typed as cleanup functions that receive an optional exception and do not return a response.
Template filter, global, and test callback types are broadened so they are not restricted to zero-argument or single-argument signatures when Flask can invoke them with arbitrary arguments.
Error-handler typing is refined so the callable's input exception type is preserved while its output remains a valid Flask response return value.
acceptance_criteria: When a developer registers a `before_request` handler that takes no arguments and returns either `None` or any supported Flask response return value, the public type hints should accept it without requiring a type override.
When a developer registers a `before_app_request` handler with the same zero-argument, optional-response behavior, the public type hints should accept it as a valid callback.
When a developer registers a `before_first_request` or `before_app_first_request` handler, the public type hints should treat it as a zero-argument callback whose return value is not used.

When a developer annotates teardown callbacks, template callbacks, or error handlers against Flask's exported typing contracts, those annotations should reflect the framework's observable invocation and return behavior rather than narrower unsupported signatures.

task_3.title: Correct Flask callback typing contracts
task_3.description: Flask 2.0.2 corrects type annotations for template globals and related callback hooks so valid application callables type-check correctly, especially when template helpers accept arguments or request hooks use their documented return behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to Flask 2.0.2 fixes inaccurate typing for template globals and related callback hooks so valid application callables are accepted by static type checkers and the exposed typing contracts match documented Flask behavior.

expectation.grounded: The typing contracts exposed through Flask for `template_global`, `template_filter`, and `template_test` should accept callables with argument signatures appropriate to their template usage instead of restricting them to zero or one fixed argument. `BeforeRequestCallable` should allow either no return value or any valid `ResponseReturnValue`. `TeardownCallable` should represent cleanup callbacks that receive an optional exception and return no value. Error handler typing should support handlers parameterized by specific `Exception` subclasses while still returning a valid `ResponseReturnValue`. A distinct `BeforeFirstRequestCallable` alias should exist for zero-argument startup hooks.
expectation.conceptual: The public typing surface should reflect how Flask hooks and template helpers actually behave. Template helpers must be free to accept the arguments they are invoked with, request hooks may either continue processing or short-circuit with a response, teardown handlers are cleanup-only, and error handlers should type-check when written for specific exception types.

constraints.grounded: This upgrade must remain a typing-level correction only, without changing runtime behavior. Existing valid Flask callback patterns should continue to be representable, including request hooks that return a normal Flask response value or `None`, teardown handlers that receive an optional exception, and template decorators that wrap variadic callables.
constraints.conceptual: The change should improve static typing accuracy without altering how applications run. Valid existing hook and template-helper patterns should continue to work, and the revised contracts should narrow only behavior that is not actually part of the public callback semantics.

behavior: Functions registered with `@app.template_global()` are treated as valid even when they accept one or more arguments.
Template filter and template test callables are typed as accepting the arguments supplied by template evaluation rather than a single rigid signature.
Before-request callbacks are typed to allow either no return value or any standard Flask response return value.
Teardown callbacks are typed as receiving an optional exception and not producing a response value.
Error handlers can be typed against specific exception subclasses while still returning any valid Flask response return value.
A dedicated zero-argument callable type is available for before-first-request handlers.
acceptance_criteria: When an application defines a template global with one or more parameters and decorates it with `@app.template_global()`, it should be accepted by static typing as a valid template global.
When an application defines a template filter or template test whose callable accepts the arguments used during template evaluation, Flask's typing should accept that callable shape.
When a before-request hook returns `None`, it should remain valid under the published typing contracts.
When a before-request hook returns any normal Flask response return value, it should also remain valid under the published typing contracts.
When a teardown hook accepts an optional exception argument and returns no value, it should match Flask's typing contract.
When an error handler is declared for a specific exception subtype, the handler should type-check as long as it returns a valid Flask response return value.

task_1.title: Correct typing for teardown and related callback decorators
task_1.description: Flask 2.0.2 corrects callback type annotations so teardown hooks are no longer treated as response-producing callbacks, and related request-hook, template, and error-handler typings better reflect the callable shapes accepted by the framework. This is intended to remove false-positive typing errors without changing runtime behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Flask's callback-based decorators and registrations are typed to match documented and existing runtime behavior, especially that `teardown_*` hooks are not required to return a response and other supported callback forms are accepted by static typing.

expectation.grounded: The `teardown_*` hook family, including decorators such as `teardown_request`, should no longer require callbacks to be typed as returning a `Response`, because teardown return values are ignored. `before_request` callbacks should allow either no return value or a normal Flask response return value. First-request hooks should remain distinct no-return callbacks. Template filter, global, and test decorators should accept callables with arbitrary argument signatures, while template tests still return booleans. Error-handler callbacks should support handlers typed for specific exception subclasses and continue to return standard Flask response return values.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to annotate Flask lifecycle hooks, template helpers, and error handlers in the same way those callbacks already behave at runtime. Teardown hooks should not be modeled as response-producing callbacks, request hooks should support their normal short-circuiting behavior, template helpers should not be restricted to a single fixed signature, and exception handlers should work with specific exception types.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the runtime contract of these APIs. Teardown callbacks must still receive an optional exception context and have their result ignored. `before_request` callbacks must still only short-circuit request handling through supported Flask response return values or by returning nothing. Error handlers must still produce normal Flask response return values. Template tests must remain boolean-valued from the caller's perspective.
constraints.conceptual: This update should only align typing with existing supported behavior. It must not alter how hooks execute, when request processing stops, what error handlers return, or how template helpers are called at runtime.

behavior: Teardown hook callbacks are treated as callbacks whose result is ignored rather than as callbacks that must return a response object.
`before_request`-style callbacks may be typed to either return nothing or return a standard Flask response value that stops normal request processing.
First-request callbacks are represented separately from per-request callbacks and remain no-return lifecycle hooks.
Template filter, template global, and template test decorators accept callables with arbitrary argument signatures instead of forcing a single fixed callable shape.
Error-handler callbacks support functions specialized to particular exception subclasses while still producing standard Flask response return values.
acceptance_criteria: When a developer annotates a teardown callback that does not return a response, the callback should be accepted by Flask's public typing.
When a developer annotates a `before_request` callback, the typing should allow either no return value or a standard Flask response return value.
When a developer registers a first-request callback, the typing should treat it as a distinct no-return lifecycle hook rather than a per-request response-capable hook.
When a developer decorates a template filter, global, or test function that takes one or more arguments, Flask's typing should accept that callable shape.
When a developer writes an error handler for a specific exception subclass, Flask's typing should accept the specialized exception parameter while preserving the normal response return contract.

task_5.title: Preserve specific exception typing in error handlers
task_5.description: The error-handler registration APIs now preserve the specific exception type associated with a handler instead of forcing handlers to accept a generic Exception. This makes `errorhandler` and `register_error_handler` align better with the actual runtime contract while keeping existing error-handler resolution behavior and slightly tightening the way invalid HTTP error-code registrations surface errors.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that registering an error handler for a specific exception class preserves that same exception type in the handler signature, instead of requiring a generic `Exception` parameter, while keeping existing error-handler registration and resolution behavior intact.

expectation.grounded: `Flask.errorhandler`, `Blueprint.errorhandler`, and `register_error_handler` should accept handlers whose argument type matches the concrete exception class used for registration. A handler registered for a specific exception subclass should be type-compatible with that subclass in its callback parameter and may still return any normal Flask `ResponseReturnValue`. Registrations by HTTP status code should continue to work, and invalid HTTP error-code registrations should still raise `ValueError`.
expectation.conceptual: When a developer registers a handler for a custom exception type, the framework should treat the handler as receiving that exact exception type rather than a generic one. Existing handler behavior for status-code-based registrations and normal Flask response returns should remain stable, and invalid error-code registrations should still fail clearly.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress the existing ability to register handlers by exception class or HTTP status code. Do not change the handler return contract. Preserve the established handler lookup precedence across blueprint-specific and application-wide handlers, including fallback from code-based to exception-class-based handling. Invalid HTTP error codes must continue to fail with `ValueError`.
constraints.conceptual: Keep current error-handling behavior stable apart from the stronger typing contract. The update must not alter which handler is selected for a given error, what kinds of responses handlers may return, or the fact that unsupported HTTP error-code registrations are rejected.

behavior: Registering a handler with `errorhandler(SomeExceptionSubclass)` should allow the handler callback to declare its error parameter as `SomeExceptionSubclass` rather than only `Exception`.
Registering a handler with `register_error_handler(SomeExceptionSubclass, handler)` should preserve the same exception subtype relationship between the registered exception and the handler parameter.
Handlers registered by HTTP status code should remain valid and continue to use the normal Flask response return contract.
Supplying an unrecognized HTTP error code to `register_error_handler` should raise `ValueError` without exposing an unrelated chained exception context.
Error-handler lookup for exceptions without an associated HTTP status code should continue to resolve the same matching handler precedence without redundant fallback passes.
acceptance_criteria: When a developer registers `app.errorhandler` for a concrete exception subclass, the handler should be accepted with that same subclass annotated as its error parameter.
When a developer registers `register_error_handler` for a concrete exception subclass, the callback should remain type-consistent with that subclass.
When a handler is registered by integer HTTP status code, it should still be usable and return any standard Flask response value.
When `register_error_handler` is given an unsupported HTTP status code, it should raise `ValueError`.
When an exception has no HTTP status code, Flask should still choose the applicable blueprint or app error handler using the existing precedence rules.

task_6.title: Preserve blueprint-local behavior across renamed registrations
task_6.description: Flask 2.0.2 fixes repeated blueprint registration so the same Blueprint can be mounted more than once under different names without losing blueprint-scoped request hooks or error handling on later registrations.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that registering the same Blueprint multiple times with different names keeps every named registration fully functional, including blueprint-scoped request preprocessing and error handling, rather than only applying that behavior to the first registration.

expectation.grounded: When `Flask.register_blueprint` is called multiple times for the same `Blueprint` instance with distinct `name` values, each registration should retain the blueprint's own callbacks registered through APIs such as `Blueprint.before_request` and `Blueprint.errorhandler`, in addition to exposing its routes under the requested prefix.
expectation.conceptual: Mounting one blueprint in more than one place should behave consistently for every mount. Later named registrations should not silently lose the blueprint's request lifecycle behavior or its custom error handling.

constraints.grounded: The fix should preserve existing registration semantics while extending blueprint-scoped behavior to every distinct blueprint name created from repeated registration of the same `Blueprint` object. It should not rely on creating duplicate blueprint objects or alter the normal requirement that separate mounts use separate names.
constraints.conceptual: This should be a non-breaking consistency fix: keep the existing multi-mount pattern, and make each named mount honor the same blueprint-local behavior instead of only the first one.

behavior: A `Blueprint` registered more than once with different `name` values should execute its blueprint-level `before_request` callbacks for requests handled by each named registration.
Blueprint-level error handlers should apply when an error is raised from any differently named registration of the same `Blueprint`, not just the first registration.
Registering the same `Blueprint` object under a new name should create a fully functional named mount whose blueprint-scoped behavior matches the original registration.
acceptance_criteria: When the same `Blueprint` instance is registered twice with different `name` values and different URL prefixes, requests routed through either prefix should trigger the blueprint's registered `before_request` callbacks.

When a view served through any named registration of that `Blueprint` raises or aborts with an error handled by the blueprint, the registered blueprint error handler should be used for every named registration.

When an application mounts a shared `Blueprint` under multiple names, the later registration should not lose blueprint-local behavior solely because the `Blueprint` object was already registered once.

task_7.title: Accept PathLike values for static_folder
task_7.description: The update broadens the public typing contract for static file configuration so `static_folder` accepts `pathlib.Path` and other path-like objects anywhere users configure it, aligning type hints with the existing path normalization behavior and preventing false type-checking failures.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that `static_folder` accepts `pathlib.Path` and other path-like values anywhere users configure static file directories, without creating type incompatibilities or changing the existing static file behavior for equivalent paths.

expectation.grounded: The `static_folder` parameter and property assignment for `Flask` and `Blueprint` should accept `None`, `str`, and `os.PathLike` inputs. Passing a `pathlib.Path` to these public APIs should be treated as valid, and the configured value should continue to follow the existing normalized string-based `static_folder` behavior exposed by the framework.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to configure static file folders with either strings or standard Python path objects in the same places they already configure `static_folder`. Using a path object should behave the same as using the equivalent string path, while also being recognized as valid by typed code.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress support for existing `str` and `None` values. Path-like inputs must preserve the current normalization semantics of `static_folder`, including conversion to the framework's existing path representation and preservation of disabled static-folder behavior when the value is `None`.
constraints.conceptual: Existing applications that pass string paths or disable static files must continue to work unchanged. Accepting path objects should add compatibility, not alter how static folders are resolved for equivalent inputs.

behavior: `Flask(..., static_folder=...)` accepts `str`, `os.PathLike`, or `None` as valid input.
`Blueprint(..., static_folder=...)` accepts `str`, `os.PathLike`, or `None` as valid input.
Assigning `static_folder` after object creation accepts `pathlib.Path` and other path-like values without a typing mismatch.
Path-like `static_folder` inputs continue through the existing normalization flow and behave the same as equivalent string paths.
Setting `static_folder` to `None` continues to represent the absence of a static folder.
acceptance_criteria: When a user passes a `pathlib.Path` value as `static_folder` while creating a `Flask` application, it should be accepted as a valid configuration and static file behavior should match the equivalent string path.

When a user passes a `pathlib.Path` value as `static_folder` while creating a `Blueprint`, it should be accepted as a valid configuration and static file behavior should match the equivalent string path.

When a user assigns a `pathlib.Path` value to `static_folder` after creation, the assignment should be accepted and the resulting static folder behavior should remain consistent with the equivalent string path.
When `static_folder` is a string, behavior should remain unchanged from prior releases.
When `static_folder` is `None`, static folder handling should remain disabled as before.
In typed user code, `pathlib.Path` values supplied to `static_folder` should no longer be treated as incompatible with the public API.

task_8.title: Restore Decimal JSON serialization
task_8.description: Version 2.0.2 restores Flask's default JSON support for decimal values by serializing decimal.Decimal instances as strings. This lets applications return or dump JSON data containing Decimal values without custom encoders or optional JSON dependencies, while preserving existing handling for other supported Flask-specific types.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Flask JSON serialization accepts decimal.Decimal values in application payloads and encodes them safely instead of failing when Decimal objects appear in JSON output.

expectation.grounded: When Flask's default JSON serialization path is used, including jsonify and flask.json.dumps through flask.json.JSONEncoder, decimal.Decimal must be treated as a supported type and serialized to a JSON string using its decimal string form. Existing supported conversions for date and datetime values, uuid.UUID, and dataclass instances should continue to work as before.
expectation.conceptual: Applications should be able to include Decimal values in JSON responses and serialized payloads without extra configuration. Decimal content should remain representable without loss from forced numeric conversion, and the rest of Flask's normal JSON behavior should stay unchanged.

constraints.grounded: Decimal support must be additive to Flask's built-in JSON encoder behavior, not a replacement for existing conversions. The observable representation of decimal.Decimal should be a JSON string, and users should not need a custom encoder or optional simplejson dependency solely to support Decimal values.
constraints.conceptual: The fix should expand default JSON compatibility for Decimal values without regressing other supported serialized types or changing how existing JSON APIs are used.

behavior: Flask's default JSON encoder recognizes decimal.Decimal as a serializable type.
Decimal values emitted through Flask JSON APIs are encoded as JSON strings rather than causing a serialization failure.
Default handling for other supported non-native types, including date-like values, UUIDs, and dataclass instances, remains intact.
acceptance_criteria: When an application serializes data containing decimal.Decimal through Flask's default JSON APIs, it should succeed without requiring a custom JSON encoder.
When a Decimal value is serialized in JSON output, it should appear as a JSON string reflecting the Decimal's string form.
When payloads contain Decimal values together with other Flask-supported special types such as datetimes, the payload should still serialize successfully under the default encoder.
When upgrading from 2.0.1 to 2.0.2, applications that previously failed only because Decimal was present in JSON data should work without adding an extra JSON library dependency.

task_9.title: Preserve original CLI loading errors during lazy app startup
task_9.description: The CLI should no longer mask deferred application-loading failures during lazy startup, and app discovery errors should surface as consistent `NoAppException` failures with clearer exception context. This makes `flask run` and related CLI loading flows report the real underlying problem instead of replacing it with misleading secondary exceptions.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that Flask CLI preserves the original exception when application loading is deferred under lazy loading, and ensure that CLI app discovery failures are reported as consistent `NoAppException` errors instead of being obscured by misleading exception handling.

expectation.grounded: When a loader used by `flask run --lazy-loading` fails, `DispatchingApp` must re-raise the original exception instance captured during background loading rather than raising a tuple-like exception payload or replacing the failure with a generic `TypeError`. During app discovery, `find_best_app`, `find_app_by_string`, and `locate_app` must continue raising `NoAppException` for invalid factory calls, parse failures, missing attributes, and import failures, while preserving relevant exception causes for invocation, attribute, and import errors and suppressing irrelevant parser traceback context for user-facing parse failures.
expectation.conceptual: Lazy CLI startup should expose the real application error that occurred, not a secondary framework error. When the CLI cannot locate, parse, import, or invoke the target app or factory, it should fail with a consistent app-loading error that points to the actual category of problem without leaking misleading exception context.

constraints.grounded: The change must not alter successful app discovery or successful lazy loading behavior. `NoAppException` must remain the user-visible failure type for CLI app lookup and invocation problems. Only the captured original loader exception should be re-raised for deferred lazy-loading failures, and parser-related `NoAppException` cases should avoid chaining unrelated low-level syntax or literal-evaluation exceptions.
constraints.conceptual: Normal startup must continue to work unchanged. The fix is limited to making failure reporting accurate and stable: genuine app-loading errors should stay genuine, and CLI lookup failures should remain clean, consistent, and non-misleading.

behavior: If background application loading fails during lazy CLI startup, the subsequent request-triggered failure surfaces the original exception type raised by the loader.
Deferred lazy-loading failures are no longer replaced by a generic exception about invalid exception objects.
If an app factory is detected but cannot be called without required arguments, CLI discovery raises `NoAppException` and retains the triggering `TypeError` as the cause.
If an app reference cannot be parsed as a valid attribute or callable expression, CLI discovery raises `NoAppException` without exposing irrelevant parser or literal-evaluation traceback context.
If the named app attribute is missing from the imported module, CLI discovery raises `NoAppException` with the underlying `AttributeError` as the cause.

If module import fails, CLI discovery raises `NoAppException`; when the import error originates inside the imported module, the original `ImportError` is preserved as the cause instead of being flattened into an unrelated secondary failure.
acceptance_criteria: When an app factory or loader raises `RuntimeError` during `flask run --lazy-loading`, the first request should fail with that `RuntimeError` rather than a generic exception about exception objects.
When lazy loading succeeds, CLI startup and request handling should behave the same as before.

When the CLI targets a factory that cannot be called with the provided arguments, it should raise `NoAppException` describing the factory invocation problem rather than exposing a bare `TypeError` as the final user-facing error.
When the CLI receives an invalid app-expression string, it should raise `NoAppException` describing the parse failure without appending unrelated parser internals to the reported failure.
When the CLI references a missing app attribute, it should raise `NoAppException` for the missing attribute condition.
When importing the target module fails, the CLI should raise `NoAppException`, and the underlying import failure should remain attributable as the cause.

task_10.title: Fix CLI app factory loading for create_app(**kwargs)
task_10.description: Version 2.0.2 fixes Flask CLI application-factory loading so factories that accept only variable keyword arguments are no longer misclassified as requiring a positional argument. This restores compatibility for dependency-injection style create_app factories while preserving the deprecated fallback for older single-parameter factories that actually accept one required positional value.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the CLI can load an application factory such as create_app that accepts only optional variable keyword arguments, without incorrectly treating it as a factory that requires an explicit positional argument.

expectation.grounded: When Flask CLI resolves an app factory through its loader, a factory like create_app(**kwargs) must be callable without explicit factory arguments. The loader must not route such a signature through the deprecated single-required-parameter compatibility path that passes script_info positionally. The deprecated positional script_info fallback should remain limited to factories with exactly one required non-VAR_KEYWORD parameter when no explicit args were supplied.
expectation.conceptual: Application factories that are designed to accept injected keyword-only dependencies through arbitrary keyword arguments should continue to load normally from the CLI. The CLI should only use its legacy single-argument compatibility behavior for factories that truly define one required positional-compatible parameter.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress the existing deprecated compatibility behavior for factories with one required non-variadic parameter and no explicit CLI factory arguments. Do not treat a lone **kwargs parameter as evidence that the factory needs a positional argument. Keep observable loader behavior aligned with the factory signature rather than introspection quirks for variadic keyword parameters.
constraints.conceptual: The fix must be narrowly scoped: restore support for flexible keyword-accepting factories without changing how genuinely single-parameter factories are handled. Signature inspection should not cause the CLI to invent unsupported positional calls.

behavior: A CLI-discovered create_app factory whose only declared parameter is **kwargs loads successfully without requiring explicit factory arguments.
The CLI no longer passes deprecated positional script context to a factory solely because its only parameter is variadic keyword capture.
The deprecated single-parameter fallback remains available only for factories with exactly one required parameter that is not a variadic keyword parameter.
acceptance_criteria: Given a configured application factory create_app(**kwargs), when the CLI loads the app without explicit factory args, then it should create the application successfully.
When the factory's only parameter is **kwargs, the CLI should not fail because of an attempted positional call to that factory.

Given a factory with exactly one required non-**kwargs parameter and no explicit factory args, when the CLI loads it, then the legacy deprecated single-argument compatibility behavior should still apply.

task_11.title: Fix Nested Blueprint Callback Ordering
task_11.description: Version 2.0.2 fixes inconsistent callback ordering for nested blueprints so request preprocessing, template context contribution, and URL default handling follow the blueprint hierarchy predictably. The change makes the application run these hooks from the app through parent blueprints to the most specific nested blueprint, while response and teardown phases unwind in the opposite direction.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that nested blueprint lifecycle callbacks execute in a consistent hierarchy order so the most specific blueprint can reliably override parent and app behavior during request handling, template rendering, and URL generation.

expectation.grounded: For routes served by nested blueprints, Flask must invoke `url_value_preprocessor`, `before_request`, template `context_processor`, and `url_defaults` functions from the application scope to the outermost blueprint and then inward to the closest nested blueprint. If a `before_request` handler returns a non-`None` value, request dispatch must stop at that point using the corrected outer-to-inner order. `after_request` and `teardown_request` callbacks must run in reverse nesting order so response handling and cleanup unwind from the closest blueprint back to the application.
expectation.conceptual: Nested blueprint hooks should behave like hierarchical scoping: setup and preprocessing flow from the app into parent and then child blueprints, and post-response cleanup flows back out. The most specific blueprint should be the final authority for request-time overrides before the view runs.

constraints.grounded: Behavior outside an active request context must remain valid for template rendering and URL building. Explicit values passed when rendering a template must continue to override values added by context processors. Ordering changes must apply to resolving nested blueprint scopes and must not alter the declared order of callbacks within the same scope.
constraints.conceptual: The fix should only correct hierarchy resolution, not break existing callback registration order or override explicit caller-provided values. Non-request usage of templating and URL generation should continue to work.

behavior: When handling a request for a nested blueprint endpoint, request preprocessors run from the app to parent blueprints and finally to the most specific nested blueprint.

Template context processors for nested blueprints merge values in that same outer-to-inner order, allowing the innermost blueprint to override parent or app-provided keys while explicit render arguments still take precedence.
URL default functions for nested blueprint endpoints apply in outer-to-inner order so the most specific blueprint can supply or override defaults last.
A non-`None` response returned by a `before_request` callback still short-circuits request handling, but the callback that wins now reflects the corrected hierarchy order.
After the view returns, response and teardown callbacks unwind from the innermost blueprint back through parent blueprints to the app.
acceptance_criteria: Given an app with parent and child blueprints that each register `before_request` handlers, when a child blueprint route is requested, the handlers should run in app, parent, child order.

Given nested blueprints that each provide the same template context key, when rendering a template during a child blueprint request, the value from the most specific blueprint should be visible unless the render call explicitly provides that key.

Given nested blueprints that register `url_value_preprocessor` or `url_defaults`, when handling or building a child blueprint endpoint, those callbacks should be applied from the app through parent blueprints to the child blueprint.

When both parent and child `before_request` handlers could terminate the request early, the parent should run before the child and the first non-`None` return in that corrected order should determine the response.

Given nested blueprints with `after_request` or `teardown_request` handlers, when a child blueprint request completes, cleanup and response mutation should run from the child blueprint outward to the app.
